newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal seen allowing short selling eventually.
newsitem.headline: Portugal seen allowing short selling eventually.

text.p: Portuguese regulators are likely to accept "short selling" eventually for institutional investors, a member of the board of the financial markets watchdog, the Securities Market Commission (CMVM), said.

"Short selling in the sense that the seller of the securities is not the actual owner but someone who has the right to dispose of the securities, will eventually be accepted in broader conditions for big institutions such as banks and, subject to more stringent requirements, mutual funds," Correia de Matos told Reuters in an interview.

"Right now, the borrowing of securities is allowed under article 66 of the Code of the Securities Market; and the opening of margin accounts by clients of broker-dealer companies was regulated by the CMVM last year," he said.
"However, short selling in the sense that someone sells securities without guaranteeing that he will be able to deliver them, will continue to be illegal," he added.
The penalty for such short selling is a fine ranging from 300,000 escudos to 150 million escudos.

Correia de Matos said that with proper regulation, short selling could contribute to the depth and stability of the financial markets. "Short selling is a flexible instrument for market professionals," he said.
Short selling is the practice whereby the seller sells securities which, at the date of the agreement for sale, it does not own but intends to acquire prior to the delivery date.
The danger of short selling is that the seller may be unable to purchase the securities in time for delivery and will therefore default on the contract.

In a wide-ranging interview about regulation of the local financial markets, Correia de Matos said he believed market manipulation and insider trading occurred in Portugal, as elsewhere, but it was hard to prove offences.
"As volume increases, it will become more difficult for individuals to rig the market," he said.
Volume on the Lisbon share market had expanded significantly in recent years as a result of privatisations and flotations and increasing foreign investor interest.
So far, no one has been convicted of insider trading or of market manipulation in Portugal, although several cases have gone to trial or been submitted to the Attorney General, Correia de Matos said.

Practices such as creating a "run" in shares, "pooling" and "churning" are illegal in Portugal, falling under article 667 of the Code of the Securities Market, which contains the definition of the crime of "market manipulation", punishable by up to two years imprisonment.

A "run" usually involves a group of people who create activity in a share, either by their own buying or selling or by spreading rumours in order to bring about a sharp increase in the price of shares.

"Pooling" arises where investors agree to set up a fund to be managed for them by a broker. The members of the pool agree that shares of a particular company will be bought and sold successively by one member of the pool to another, through the selected broker to boost reported turnover and price. Reports of the increased activity may result in the share prices rising.

"Churning" occurs when a trader acquires a holding of shares and then places buying and selling orders for them, usually at about the same price or at slightly rising prices, in order to build up the turnover. The purchases and sales following the initial purchase operate to balance each other so that the particular trader does not suffer a loss. The report of the various sales of these shares to the stock exchange will indicate active trading in the shares, often leading to wide investor interest and further increases in the price of shares.

Correia de Matos said that in Portugal the penalties for insider trading, which involves dealing in securities using price-sensitive information that is not generally available, were jail sentences of up to two years.

He said the CMVM was preparing bilateral agreements with foreign regulators and hoped to sign a memorandum of understanding with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission later this year for the exchange of information and mutual assistance.
The CMVM had already signed similar agreements with several European and South American regulators, he said.
